evidence: app/models/blocked_email.rb:12-16 loads the row, does `record.match_count += 1` in Ruby, then `record.save`. Rails issues `UPDATE ... SET match_count = <value computed in Ruby>`, so two concurrent signups with the same blocked email can both read N and both write N+1, losing an increment. Nothing guards against this: no lock, no increment_counter/update_all. The migration (db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:54) only sets a default of 0. The race is real. The impact is small because match_count is only a stats counter, and the block decision at line 18 reads action_type, not the count. The fix is cheap: an atomic `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(['match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now])` or `record.increment!`-style SQL. Worth doing, but not a correctness blocker.

app/models/blocked_email.rb:16 ignores the return value of `record.save`, but in practice save cannot return false here. The record was just loaded from the DB, so `email` is present. set_defaults (line 3, 21-23) guarantees action_type. Uniqueness validation (line 5) excludes the record's own id. So the validations that make save return false cannot fail. Real DB errors raise exceptions instead of returning false, so they would not be silently ignored. The only data at stake is the match_count/last_match_at stats. The blocking result (line 18) does not depend on the save. Raising here (save!) would turn a stats-write problem into a signup failure inside EmailValidator (lib/validators/email_validator.rb:38). There is no real 'inconsistent data' scenario.
